source.title: Imaging with LINC-NIRVANA, the Fizeau interferometer of the Large Binocular Telescope: state of the art and open problems

accepted.question_text: How can image reconstruction for LINC-NIRVANA, the Fizeau interferometer of the Large Binocular Telescope, be extended from a space-invariant point-spread-function model to a space-variant point-spread-function model? In this setting, multiple deconvolution combines several interferometric images of the same astronomical target; the point-spread function can change with baseline orientation, adaptive-optics correction, and position in the field of view. A self-contained solution should estimate point-spread-function variation across the field from available star images, partition the image into domains where each point-spread function can be treated as approximately space-invariant, correct boundary effects inside those domain reconstructions, and recombine the results into a mosaic.

For LINC-NIRVANA multiple-image deconvolution with Poisson data, what regularization methods based on sparse representations in an appropriate basis or frame can improve reconstruction of complex astronomical objects beyond the regularization functions already tested for simpler objects such as open star clusters, nebulae, distant galaxies, and planetary surfaces?

How can LINC-NIRVANA image reconstruction recover high-dynamic-range astronomical scenes in which bright point sources are superimposed on diffuse faint structure, such as a bright star lying on top of a diffuse cloud in young stellar object observations? Existing adaptive regularization handles separated bright and faint components only when there is a large brightness difference and angular separation, so the unresolved case is reconstruction when the bright source and diffuse emission overlap.

evidence.quote: bright star over a diffuse cloud

accepted.question_text: How can the iterative reconstruction algorithms used for LINC-NIRVANA multiple-image deconvolution be accelerated in a mathematically justified and computationally efficient way? The target algorithms include Richardson-Lucy and ordered-subsets expectation-maximization variants for large astronomical images, where sufficiently bright objects can require thousands of iterations and 2048 x 2048 pixel images can take hours; existing acceleration methods need convergence guarantees and better behavior in critical cases.

How can blind or myopic deconvolution for LINC-NIRVANA be made mathematically sound and computationally efficient when the point-spread functions are unknown or only partly known? The formulation should jointly estimate the astronomical object and the point-spread functions under physical constraints such as nonnegativity, band-limiting, and known Strehl-ratio information, and should exploit the relationship between this deconvolution problem and nonnegative matrix factorization to obtain convergence analysis and practical reconstruction algorithms.
